claims.text: The quality and formation process of the native oxide layer govern the corrosion resistance of Q235 steel.
The as-received native oxide film on Q235 steel may be heterogeneous in thickness and composition.
Removing the native film and applying controlled low-temperature oxidation will form a more uniform, defect-minimized oxide film on Q235 steel.
Oxide-film integrity, thickness, phase composition, uniformity, and defect density are the structural mediators of corrosion protection.
A uniform, well-adherent oxide film acts as a barrier against ionic diffusion and corrosive attack.
At room temperature, both native and controlled oxide films may provide sufficient protection because ion mobility is low.
At high temperature, nonuniform or defective oxide films are prone to breakdown, void formation, detachment, or spallation.
Breakdown or spallation of a defective oxide film leads to accelerated corrosion of Q235 steel.
The controlled re-formed oxide will have lower defect density and greater physical integrity than the native oxide.
The controlled re-formed oxide will retard scale spallation and mass change.
At room temperature, the native-oxide and controlled-oxide samples will show minimal differences in corrosion performance.
At 700–900 °C in aggressive molten salt, the controlled-oxide samples will show less mass change and less scale spallation than native-oxide samples.
The proposed comparison holds primarily when oxide preparation is the only altered variable and may not transfer to substrates with modified bulk composition or substantial Mn or Cr changes.
The protective effect of the re-formed oxide should dominate when chemical attack and thermal cycling are both significant.
Paired native-oxide and controlled-oxide Q235 samples can be compared using mass change, SEM/EDS, XPS or ellipsometry, and electrochemical measurements.
A lack of improved high-temperature corrosion performance despite a verified improvement in oxide quality would falsify the proposed causal role of oxide quality.
